title: When memory fades
hook: Emerson at a friend's coffin: the name was gone, the kindness wasn't
tomorrow: why would a dying man remember he owed someone a rooster?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epictetus: lameness stops the leg, not the will. A body can lose a skill and the one who chooses stays. Today it isn't a leg that goes. It's the names.

A photo lands in a family group chat: a grandmother in a cardigan, and under it, she didn't know my name today, but she asked if I'd eaten. There's an older version of that text. The story is told of Ralph Waldo Emerson in his last years, when words had started slipping away from him. Reaching for the word umbrella, he'd come out with the thing that strangers take away. At the funeral of his old friend, the poet Longfellow, he stood looking at the face in the coffin and said, as the story goes, that this gentleman was a sweet, beautiful soul, but he had entirely forgotten his name.
screen: `SHE ASKED IF I'D EATEN.` → `EMERSON, LOSING HIS WORDS.` → `A SWEET, BEAUTIFUL SOUL.` → `THE NAME WAS GONE.`

segments.voice: So the name was gone. Look at what wasn't. Emerson couldn't say who his friend was, but he could still say what he was: sweet, beautiful, a soul. Long before, in an essay called The Over-Soul, Emerson had written about exactly this. The soul in a person, he said, "is not a function, like the power of memory, of calculation, of comparison, but uses these as hands and feet." That's a thread through Emerson's Transcendentalism: underneath the mind's tools is a soul, one he believed every person shares in, the Over-Soul. Memory is a hand. The soul is the one using it. So when the hand weakens, by Emerson's own teaching, the soul hasn't left. At the coffin, the tool for names was failing, and the love still worked. That's what this path takes from him: when memory fades, in someone you love or someday in you, don't measure the person by what they can recall. Notice what still comes through. Being gentle with memory means no quizzing. Not, do you know who I am? Just, it's good to see you.
screen: `HE COULD STILL SAY WHAT HE WAS.` · `THE SOUL IS NOT THE MEMORY.` · `IT USES MEMORY LIKE HANDS AND FEET.` · `NO QUIZZING: IT'S GOOD TO SEE YOU.` · then, large: `KINDNESS STAYS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose memory is fading, or simply someone older you love. For a few slow breaths, set aside what they've forgotten and name, silently, one kindness of theirs that's still there. If no one comes to mind, turn it toward yourself: one thing you keep forgetting, met gently.
When memory fades: names and facts slip, and in Emerson's teaching the soul that used them doesn't. What comes through is the kindness.
Your line: kindness stays. The name went first, and the sweet, beautiful soul stayed. Day three of seven, done.

howItsDone: People who take this from Emerson greet someone whose memory is fading warmly instead of quizzing them, and look for what still comes through: kindness, humor, care.
